---
title: "Get started with greenwood"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 96
)
```

Greenwood is a toolkit for survival analysis: the study of how long it takes for an event to
happen, when some of the times are still unknown. This article walks through a typical analysis
of the `lung` data, a trial of patients with advanced lung cancer that comes with the package.

```{r}
library(greenwood)
head(lung)
```

## The survival response

`time` is the follow-up in days and `status` is 1 for a censored patient (alive at last contact)
and 2 for a death. `Surv()` combines them into a survival response, with a `+` marking each
censored time.

```{r}
Surv(lung$time[1:8], lung$status[1:8])
```

The estimators and models take the response on the left of a formula.

## Survival curves

`kaplan_meier()` estimates the probability of surviving past each time. With a grouping
variable on the right of the formula, it estimates one curve per group.

```{r}
fit <- kaplan_meier(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
fit
```

Every table of estimates starts with a `strata` column, which is `"all"` for a fit without
groups, so the layout doesn't depend on the number of curves.

```{r}
head(as.data.frame(fit))
predict(fit, times = c(180, 365))
```

`plot_survival()` draws the curves with their confidence bands and censoring marks, and can
stack the numbers at risk underneath.

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_survival(fit, risk_table = TRUE, times = c(0, 250, 500, 750, 1000))
```

## Comparing groups

The log-rank test asks whether the groups' survival differs. The restricted mean survival time
compares the average survival up to a horizon, which is easier to interpret.

```{r}
logrank_test(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
rmst_test(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung, tau = 365)
```

## Cox regression

`cox_ph()` models the hazard as a baseline hazard multiplied by the exponential of a linear
combination of covariates. `tidy()` gives the coefficients as a data frame, and `glance()` gives
the model's summary statistics in one row.

```{r}
cox <- cox_ph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = lung)
cox
tidy(cox, exponentiate = TRUE)
glance(cox)
```

`plot_forest()` plots the hazard ratios.

```{r, fig.height = 2.5}
plot_forest(cox, term_labels = c(age = "Age", sex = "Female", ph.ecog = "ECOG score"))
```

The model assumes that each hazard ratio is constant over time. `cox_zph()` tests the assumption,
and `plot_schoenfeld()` shows the scaled Schoenfeld residuals: a flat smooth supports it.

```{r}
cox_zph(cox)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_schoenfeld(cox)
```

`smooth_hr()` checks whether a continuous covariate's effect is linear, by refitting the model
with a spline in its place.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_smooth_hr(smooth_hr(cox, term = "age"), scale = "hr")
```

`plot_predicted_survival()` shows the model's survival curves for new patients.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
patients <- data.frame(age = c(60, 60), sex = c(1, 2), ph.ecog = c(1, 1))
plot_predicted_survival(cox, patients, labels = c("Male, 60", "Female, 60"))
```

## Competing risks

When one kind of event prevents another, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of each overstates its
probability. In the `mgus2` data, patients can progress to a plasma cell malignancy or die first.
A factor response with the censoring level first gives a competing-risks response, and
`aalen_johansen()` estimates each cause's cumulative incidence.

```{r}
mgus <- data.frame(
  time = with(mgus2, ifelse(pstat == 1, ptime, futime)),
  event = factor(
    with(mgus2, ifelse(pstat == 1, 1, 2 * death)),
    levels = 0:2,
    labels = c("censor", "progression", "death")
  ),
  sex = mgus2$sex
)
cif <- aalen_johansen(Surv(time, event) ~ sex, data = mgus)
grays_test(Surv(time, event) ~ sex, data = mgus)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_cif(cif)
```

`fine_gray()` models the covariates' effects on one cause's cumulative incidence.

```{r}
tidy(fine_gray(Surv(time, event) ~ sex, data = mgus, cause = "progression"))
```

## Checking predictions

`concordance_index()` measures how well a risk score ranks the patients: 0.5 is no better than
chance, and 1 orders every comparable pair correctly. On the data the model was fit to, it's
optimistic. `cross_validate()` measures it on folds that the model didn't see.

```{r}
complete <- na.omit(lung[c("time", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog")])
cox <- cox_ph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = complete)
concordance_index(Surv(complete$time, complete$status), risk = predict(cox))

set.seed(1)
cross_validate(cox_ph, Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = complete, k = 5)
```

`brier_score()`, `time_dependent_auc()`, and `calibration()` assess predicted survival
probabilities at chosen times.
